findings.headline: Waste collection and disposal costs £500k over budget due to volumes and fuel surcharges, with further volatility expected
findings.detail: Total waste collection and disposal cost £14.338m in 2025/26, £500k over budget driven by increased volumes and fuel surcharges. Council has retained £600k contingency for ongoing waste contract volatility in reserves, indicating officers expect these pressures to persist.
findings.matters: Cost pressures in a major service budget signal either unplanned demand growth or exposure to uncontrolled commodity/fuel costs, either of which could require future budget adjustments if they persist.
findings.figures: £500k overspend on waste contracts; total waste cost £14.338m; £600k contingency retained for volatility
findings.quote: Waste Contracts are £500k over budget due to increasing volumes and fuel surcharges

findings.headline: £711m capital programme ongoing with £13.882m transferred from operating budget and surpluses in 2025/26 alone to finance strategic leisure and community projects
findings.detail: Council is executing a multi-year capital strategy, particularly for strategic leisure facilities at Templemore and Strabane alongside community projects. In 2025/26, £13.882m was transferred from capital budget (£7.874m), leisure budgets (£1.827m), and investment income (£1.081m) to cover commitments. This strategy is designed to minimise future borrowing by using operating surpluses.
findings.matters: Large capital commitments create future servicing costs and borrowing obligations. If project costs overrun or revenues underperform, the council may need to either increase borrowing or draw further on reserves at a time when reserves are already declining.
findings.figures: £711m ongoing programme; £13.882m transferred to reserves in 2025/26 (£7.874m capital, £1.827m leisure, £1.081m investment income); funded by 1.5% rates investment
findings.quote: Council's capital budget has been fully utilised in financing Council's ongoing and live £711m programme of investment.

findings.headline: District Fund reserves scheduled to decline from 8.57% to 5.97% of net expenditure by 2029/30, requiring 0.3% rates increase by 2027/28
findings.detail: Council is executing a planned reserves reduction strategy, drawing down District Fund from £7.015m (8.57% of budget) to £5.815m (5.97%) over four years. The £243k surplus this year was partly achieved by avoiding the planned £900k draw-down. By 2027/28, additional 0.3% rates investment will be needed; this same challenge repeats through 2028/29 and 2029/30.
findings.matters: Declining reserve buffers reduce financial flexibility for unexpected pressures. The target 5–7.5% guidance means the council will be at the minimum threshold, with limited capacity to absorb additional income shocks from rates appeals or grant cuts.
findings.quote: This current projection requires a 0.3% rates investment as part of the 2027/28 rates process and beyond which will be a challenge.

findings.headline: Non-domestic revaluation appeals have permanently eroded £3.5m of annual rates income, with 108 live appeals presenting further downside risk
findings.detail: Since 2023, 575 revaluation appeals concluded with average 22.5% value reduction, causing £3.5m permanent loss to recurrent income (4.4% of rates). A further 108 live appeals with £7.72m NAV could cost another £600k if similar outcomes occur, plus backdated rebates potentially exceeding £1.8m. This is described as Council's most critical funding source.
findings.matters: Rates are the council's primary income stream (£80m of £82m budget). Structural erosion from appeals directly threatens revenue sustainability and forces reliance on reserves or rates rises.
findings.figures: £3.5m recurrent loss from 575 concluded appeals; 108 live appeals with £7.72m NAV; potential additional loss £600k + rebates >£1.8m; £2.0m contingency provision retained
findings.quote: 575 appeals have been concluded with the average outcome being a 22.5% value reduction. This has resulted in a very significant loss of over £3.5m recurrent rates income to Council (circa 4.4% rates impact).

findings.paper_title: 8 Appendix A Derry City & Strabane 2025-26 Audit Strategy
findings.headline: New EPR grant funding received with undefined conditions and potential clawback mechanisms
findings.detail: The council received Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) initiative funding in 2025-26 intended to cover net efficient costs of household packaging waste management. However, specific grant conditions, restrictions, and clawback mechanisms remain unspecified, creating contingent liability uncertainty.
findings.matters: Undefined grant clawback conditions create contingent liability risk—the council could face unexpected funding recovery demands if it fails to meet unstated conditions, affecting cash flow and reserves.
findings.figures: Amount of EPR funding received not disclosed in this strategy document.
findings.quote: The specific grant conditions, restrictions, or clawback mechanisms associated with this funding have not been fully clarified.

findings.paper_title: 8 Appendix A Derry City & Strabane 2025-26 Audit Strategy
findings.headline: Significant audit risk assessed in service revenue recognition, specifically non-rates income streams
findings.detail: Auditors have identified fraud in revenue recognition as a significant risk specific to the council's non-rates service income. This triggers substantive testing including verification of income to supporting documentation, analytical review of variances, and procedures testing service income controls.
findings.matters: Flagging a revenue stream as a significant fraud risk indicates internal controls over income recognition are weak enough to warrant special audit concern—a governance red flag for lenders.
findings.figures: No amount specified for non-rates service income in this document.
findings.quote: We have assessed this risk to be significant in relation to the Council's non rates service income streams.

findings.paper_title: 8 Appendix A Derry City & Strabane 2025-26 Audit Strategy
findings.headline: Going concern review of airport subsidiary indicates financial viability concerns
findings.detail: The auditors will conduct a specific going concern assessment of CODA (Operations) Limited, the council's airport subsidiary. This is flagged as an ongoing review matter through certification, indicating concerns about the airport's ability to continue operating as a going concern.
findings.matters: A council-owned airport requiring going concern scrutiny represents a material subsidiary risk—councils with troubled airport operations often face unexpected capital calls or asset impairments.
findings.figures: No figures disclosed in strategy document; airport asset value and operating position not specified.
findings.quote: We will continue to review the progress made in respect of the financial viability of the airport to satisfy going concern consideration up to the date we certify the financial statements.

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.headline: Potential need for further unplanned rates investment in 2028/29 if project costs rise or risks materialise
findings.detail: The council explicitly flags that 'any increases to project budgets either through increased project scope or risks materialising will also have an impact on affordability and there is potential that further rates investment will be required in 2028/29 to complete the project capital financing- this would have a knock-on effect on the civic/commercial offices financing plan.' Current project risks are noted but not quantified.
findings.matters: The leisure projects are being delivered at a time of inflationary pressure and supply chain volatility. The council has identified that scope creep or risk materialisation could force unplanned additional rates calls, potentially squeezing other priorities including planned civic office development.
findings.figures: 1.5% rates investment already committed through 2027/28; potential additional 1.5% (approx £1.15m) required 2028/29
findings.quote: Despite the best efforts of Council officers, given the nature of capital projects and particularly in the current inflationary environment, there will always be an element of uncertainty around the delivery of the capital programme against the original plan. Any increases to project budgets either through increased project scope or risks materialising will also have an impact on affordability and there is potential that further rates investment will be required in 2028/29

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.headline: External funding environment deteriorating with rates-dependent strategy required through at least 2028/29
findings.detail: The council states 'external funding opportunities have become significantly more challenging in recent times due to Government budgetary constraints.' Of the £711m capital programme, £444m has been or is targeted from external sources. Beyond current commitments, the council has only £3.023m for project development with £27.423m of investment targeted but not secured.
findings.matters: As grants dry up, the council must finance capital ambitions through rates increases and borrowing. This reduces financial flexibility and increases exposure to local economic conditions and rate-payer resistance.
findings.figures: Of £711m programme: £444m from external sources targeted/secured; £3.023m development funding for projects with £30.456m total cost; unmet funding £27.423m
findings.quote: Whilst Council will continue to explore all possible external funding opportunities, the external funding environment has become much more challenging and it is clear that Council's strategy of 1.5% rates investment into it's capital programme will be required beyond 2027/28 to ensure continued progress across remaining priorities.

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.headline: PWLB interest rate sensitivity directly affects project affordability by up to £7m
findings.detail: At 6% interest over 40 years, the council can borrow £139m. At 6.50%, only £132m. Current PWLB rates on 23 January 2026 are 6.16%. The council is exploring the National Wealth Fund to save 0.4% but notes this facility is 'subject to criteria' which could mean 'part/all of the required borrowing may not be available from this source.'
findings.matters: A 75 basis point move in interest rates directly reduces available finance and directly threatens affordability of the leisure projects. This is a material live risk with limited mitigation options secured.
findings.figures: At 5.75% interest: £143m available; at 6%: £139m; at 6.50%: £132m (£11m range). Current rates 6.16%.
findings.quote: As an example, at the initial targeted 6% interest over 40 years, this would enable Council to borrow £119m plus cash reserves of £20m, leaving the total available for the projects at £139m. PWLB interest rates are linked to Government gilt rates which have been volatile due to economic and UK budget uncertainty.

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement projected to more than double to £101.8m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council's CFR is forecast to grow from £47.2m in the current year to £101.8m by 2028/29, with corresponding gross borrowing rising from £31.6m to £99.7m. This sharp increase reflects the strategic leisure projects and other capital commitments. The council remains in an under-borrowed position but this trajectory suggests increasing reliance on debt.
findings.matters: A doubling of the financing requirement signals a structural change in the council's balance sheet. It reflects growing capital intensity and suggests sustained high capital spending is now embedded in the council's plans.
findings.figures: CFR current year £47.2m, Year +3 (2028/29) £101.8m; Gross borrowing current £31.6m, Year +3 £99.7m
findings.quote: The Council's cumulative outstanding amount of debt finance is measured by the Capital Financing Requirement. This represents Council's underlying need to borrow. Council currently maintains an under-borrowed position meaning the underlying need to borrow because of capital expenditure has not been fully financed by loans.

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.headline: New leisure facilities face £465k annual revenue shortfall, potentially rising to £1m by 2030
findings.detail: The Templemore and Foyle Arena facilities combined show a revenue shortfall of £465k at 2025/26 costs and prices. The council estimates this could rise to circa £1m by 2030 due to 3% inflation, representing a further 1.25% rates implication. The pricing strategy to address this gap has only just begun through a newly-formed Pricing Working Group and remains unresolved.
findings.matters: New capital projects must be revenue-neutral or supportive. A £1m annual shortfall by 2030 represents a permanent structural deficit requiring ongoing rates support and limits headroom for other services.
findings.figures: Current shortfall £465k, forecast £1m by 2030 based on 3% inflation, represents 1.25% rates implication
findings.quote: Based on current costs and prices (i.e. if these facilities were to open in 2025/26), there would be a revenue shortfall of £465k. This figure will increase due to pay and cost inflation between now and the facilities being opened. As an estimate, based on 3% inflation, the revenue shortfall could equate to circa £1m by 2030- this would represent a further 1.25% rates implication.

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.headline: Two major strategic leisure projects need £143.91m of council funding, with no funding fully secured
findings.detail: The Strabane leisure centre requires £42.804m total capital cost and Templemore £101.271m. Together they face a £143.91m financing requirement after accounting for limited external funding already secured. The council has secured £120m through 2026/27 rates investment but explicitly states 'a further 1.5% rates investment required in 2027/28 to complete the funding packages for these projects.'
findings.matters: This represents a major multi-year capital commitment requiring sustained rates investment and borrowing. Any slippage, cost inflation, or changed circumstances could force difficult choices about project scope or rates.
findings.figures: Strabane £42.804m, Templemore £101.271m, combined funding gap £143.91m, £120m secured via rates investment to 2026/27, further £16m-£18m rates investment required 2027/28
findings.quote: Subject to resolution of reported project risks as well as interest rates sensitivities and movements, the 2026/27 rates investment will mean that circa £120m of this financing requirement has now been secured with a further 1.5% rates investment required in 2027/28 to complete the funding packages for these projects

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.paper_title: Report 2 Appendix 2 Prudential and Treasury M I 2026 27
findings.headline: Authorised borrowing limits rise from £35m to £104m over three years
findings.detail: The operational boundary for external debt grows from £35m (2025/26) to £104m (2028/29), and authorised limits from £38m to £107m. These increases accommodate both projected borrowing and the addition of IFRS 16 lease liabilities (£2–3m across the period).
findings.matters: Large upward revisions to debt limits signal a significant change in financial structure. While statutory procedures allow these increases, the scale suggests the council is entering a higher-leverage phase.
findings.figures: Operational Limit Total External Debt: 35.0m (2025/26), 46.0m (2026/27), 59.0m (2027/28), 104.0m (2028/29); Authorised Limit: 38.0m, 49.0m, 62.0m, 107.0m
findings.quote: Operational Limit – Total External Debt 35.0m 46.0m 59.0m 104.0m; Authorised Limit – Total External Debt 38.0m 49.0m 62.0m 107.0m

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.paper_title: Report 2 Appendix 2 Prudential and Treasury M I 2026 27
findings.headline: Capital financing costs rise to 20.2% of net revenue stream by 2028/29
findings.detail: Financing costs (capital-related revenue charges including minimum revenue provision) increase from 17.3% (2025/26) to 20.2% (2028/29), reflecting the growing debt burden and principal repayment requirements.
findings.matters: A financing cost ratio above 20% is manageable but constrains discretionary spending. Lenders assess whether this leaves headroom for other pressures and whether the council can hit rates targets.
findings.quote: Estimates of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream...19.3% 17.3% 17.7% 18.9% 20.2%

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.paper_title: Report 2 Appendix 2 Prudential and Treasury M I 2026 27
findings.headline: Council transitions from treasury investor to borrower in medium term
findings.detail: Liability benchmark analysis shows the council currently holds cash available to invest. However, projected capital expenditure will require the council to shift to net borrowing within 2–3 years as capital plans accelerate and reserves deplete.
findings.matters: A shift from cash position to borrowing changes the council's financial risk profile and may affect its ability to absorb shocks. The timing and scale of this transition matters for prudential management.
findings.figures: Liability benchmark chart showing current cash position versus medium-term borrowing requirement
findings.quote: From the graph below it is evident Council currently has cash to invest in the short term but based on current projections, there will be a borrowing requirement in the medium term.

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.paper_title: Report 2 Appendix 2 Prudential and Treasury M I 2026 27
findings.headline: Borrowing requirement spikes 23-fold in 2028/29 after two years of modest levels
findings.detail: Planned borrowing sits at £1.9m (2026/27) and £16.5m (2027/28) before jumping to £44.2m (2028/29). The increase reflects the capital programme accelerating and grant funding reducing as a proportion of total financing.
findings.matters: This concentration of new borrowing in the outer years creates execution and market risk. If capital projects slip or grants are delayed, the council faces higher refinancing costs or cash shortfalls.

findings.committee: Special Meeting of Derry City and Strabane District Council
findings.paper_title: Report 2 Appendix 2 Prudential and Treasury M I 2026 27
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement nearly doubles to £101.8m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The CFR grows from £44.7m (actual 2024/25) to £46.4m (2026/27) then accelerates to £60.4m (2027/28) and £101.8m (2028/29). This reflects a planned capital programme growing from £28.1m to £55.1m over the same period, driven by infrastructure projects including leisure centre replacements and public realm schemes.
findings.matters: A doubling of the underlying borrowing requirement signals a major structural shift in capital intensity and financial position. Lenders need to understand whether this is sustainable and properly funded.
findings.quote: Capital Financing Requirement 44.7m 47.2m 46.4m 60.4m 101.8m [across prior year and four year forecast]
